It reflects a broader shift. In a more uncertain global environment, organisations are reassessing how their buildings perform under stress - not just operationally, but physically.

One area that is often underestimated is glazing.

In the event of an explosion or shockwave, a significant proportion of injuries are caused not by the initial event itself, but by flying glass and internal fragmentation. 𝟵𝟵% 𝗼𝗳 𝗶𝗻𝗷𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗴𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘀 𝗳𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀. 

As a result, more businesses are taking a proactive view of their duty of care looking at how to better protect staff, visitors and the internal fabric of their workplaces, while also ensuring continuity in the aftermath of an incident.
We specialise in blast containment window film systems designed to hold glass in place under extreme conditions. These solutions are discreet, retrofit-ready and engineered to reduce risk without compromising the integrity or appearance of the building. 

This is not about reacting to events. It’s about preparing environments to perform when it matters most. For organisations reviewing resilience and protection strategies, glazing is increasingly part of that conversation.

posts.commentary:
There is no shortage of data centre construction underway but what is less visible and increasingly felt on site is the gap between volume and capability.

As demand accelerates, the pressure on electrical delivery is becoming more apparent. Not in numbers, but in standards.

As our Technical Operations Manager, @[Gavin Bannerman](urn:li:person:y0E9qox69A) says:

“It’s not a labour shortage. It’s a standards shortage and you can feel the difference the moment you step onto site.”

There is a clear difference between installation and execution at a level that stands up to inspection, integrates into complex power architectures and supports smooth commissioning.

In mission-critical environments, that gap becomes costly. Delays, rework, incomplete documentation - these are rarely resource issues. They are indicators of capability.

We take a managed approach to delivery. Our teams are selected, led and deployed with a clear understanding of the environments they operate in. Accountable, technically aligned and structured to meet the standards our clients expect.

As the sector continues to scale, the conversation is shifting. It’s no longer about how quickly capacity can be built but how well it is delivered.

posts.commentary:
This legislation establishes a clear and consistent expectation: safeguarding people is not optional nor can it be left open to interpretation.

Martyn’s Law represents a fundamental shift in how responsibility for public safety is both defined and enforced.

In high-value, high-occupancy environments; whether public venues, commercial assets or mission-critical facilities the consequences of underestimating risk are significant. What this legislation brings is long-overdue structure and accountability across the industry.

The focus now turns to readiness.

Understanding the requirements is one part of the equation and implementing them effectively within live, complex environments is another.  Those who take a proactive, considered approach will be far better positioned than those reacting under pressure.

Take a look through the carousel to understand what Martyn’s Law involves, and how to begin preparing your environment.

 • Handover isn’t delayed by avoidable issues

Technical cleaning is built into the delivery process. Our teams operate to clean-build and ISO-aligned standards, supporting projects through to a fully compliant, commissioning-ready state.

posts.commentary:
In many buildings, security strategies focus on access control, surveillance and perimeter protection. Far less attention is given to the performance of the glazing itself.

In the City of London, we supported a high-net-worth client with the installation of anti-bandit and blast containment window films - a deliberate step to address one of the most vulnerable elements of any façade.
In the event of an incident, glass can become the primary source of injury and internal damage. By integrating containment solutions, the client is strengthening their environment in a way that protects people, preserves the internal fabric of the building and reflects a clear sense of responsibility towards those who occupy it.

There is a noticeable shift in how leading organisations are thinking about risk with glazing now recognised as a key part of a wider resilience strategy.

Security risk is evolving, both in frequency and in nature. What was once considered isolated is now far more widespread, affecting commercial spaces, public-facing environments and high-profile individuals alike.

As a result, organisations are taking a more considered approach to how their buildings perform under threat.

We work with safety, security and blast containment window films designed to strengthen glazing under impact. When applied, these systems help hold shattered glass in place, reducing the risk of injury from fragmentation and providing an additional barrier against forced entry.

In higher-risk environments, our blast mitigation solutions are engineered to reduce glass fallout following shockwave exposure, supporting recognised safety standards and improving occupant protection.

These are discreet, cost-effective interventions but their impact is significant. Increasingly, glazing is being recognised not just as a design feature, but as a critical component of a building’s overall security strategy.
